prompt: Match each change to the kind of scaling it is.

pairs.left: Moving from 4 cores to 64 in one server
Spreading a table across eight nodes
Starting compute for month-end, reading the same files

prompt: According to the lesson's rule of thumb, when is one machine the simpler answer?

choices.text: When its working data fits in memory
choices.why: Right. Past that point, scaling out starts to pay.

choices.text: When the warehouse has fewer than a million rows
choices.why: Row counts alone say little; it is what a query reads that matters.

choices.text: When there is a single analyst
choices.why: Users affect concurrency, not whether one machine can hold the data.

choices.text: When the data is in PostgreSQL
choices.why: The engine is not the test.

prompt: With one thread the query took 0.358 s and with four 0.126 s. How many times as fast was it with four? Give one decimal.
hint: Divide the first by the second.

prompt: Why did four threads not make the query four times as fast?
hint: Not every part of a query splits.

choices.text: DuckDB only uses two threads
choices.why: The `user` time with four threads shows more than two were busy.

choices.text: The table was too small to split
choices.why: 17.7 million rows split well; the serial part is the limit.

choices.text: Part of the work is serial
choices.why: Right. Starting, building lookups and merging partial sums do not split.

choices.text: Each thread read the whole table
choices.why: Then more threads would have been slower, not faster.

prompt: A job is 90% parallel. Using Amdahl's law, what is its speed-up on 4 processors? Give one decimal.
A job is 95% parallel. What is the highest speed-up any number of processors can give it?
A distributed query's nodes spend half their time exchanging rows over the network. What happens as more nodes are added?
hint: The exchange is part of the serial share.

choices.text: It scales without limit, because each node has less data
choices.why: Less data per node shrinks the parallel part only.

choices.text: The gains flatten out quickly
choices.why: Right. With half the time serial, the ceiling is about 2.

choices.text: It gets slower at once
choices.why: Not at once; it stops improving.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because networks are free
choices.why: Moving rows is the cost the lesson is about.

prompt: The grouping finished with the machine's memory, finished more slowly with 200 MB, and failed with 20 MB. What does that show?

choices.text: DuckDB has a bug at small memory limits
choices.why: It behaved as designed and said what it needed.

choices.text: Memory affects only the speed of a query, never whether it runs
choices.why: The 20 MB run did not complete.

choices.text: 200 MB was faster than the full memory
choices.why: It was slower: 0.466 s against 0.340 s.

choices.text: Less memory slows it; far less stops it
choices.why: Right. That is the shape of the ceiling on one machine.

prompt: Which of these are limits of a single machine named in the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The largest machine you can buy is a fixed size
choices.why: Yes. Memory, disk and network all top out.

choices.text: It is a single point of failure
choices.why: Yes. When it is down, the warehouse is down.

choices.text: It is sized for the busiest hour and idle the rest
choices.why: Yes. Paid for all month.

choices.text: It cannot run SQL joins
choices.why: It runs them fine.

prompt: Put the steps of a query on a shared-nothing system in order.
items: The coordinator plans and sends each node its part
Each node scans and sums its own rows
The partial results are merged into one answer
trap: Merging before every node has finished is impossible: the query is as slow as its slowest node.

prompt: For "total revenue by department" on four nodes, what crosses the network?
hint: Each node sums its own share.

choices.text: Every sales row, to the coordinator
choices.why: That would be the opposite of the design.

choices.text: Half of each node's rows
choices.why: No row needs to move for this query.

choices.text: Four partial sums per node
choices.why: Right. The data stays; only the answers move.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: The partial sums have to reach the coordinator.

prompt: A system where each node has its own processors, memory and share of the data, and reads no other node's disk, is called ___ nothing.
hint: What the nodes do not do with each other.

prompt: Why did spreading sales by order number give four nearly equal nodes?

choices.text: There are hundreds of thousands of them
choices.why: Right. Many values, spread evenly.

choices.text: Order numbers are sequential
choices.why: The hash scatters them; their order does not matter.

choices.text: Every order has the same number of lines
choices.why: Orders have one to six lines; it evens out over many orders.

choices.text: DuckDB balances the nodes on purpose
choices.why: The nodes here are a hash and a count.

prompt: Spread by shop, the fullest node got 643,004 of the 887,477 rows. What percentage is that? Give a whole number.
hint: Divide and multiply by a hundred.

prompt: A cluster has one node per shop, seven nodes. Why is it still skewed?

choices.text: Seven is an odd number of nodes, and hashing needs an even one
choices.why: Hashing works with any number of nodes.

choices.text: Moinhos opened in 2025
choices.why: It is a small node; the problem is the large one.

choices.text: Each shop has a different number of books
choices.why: Rows are sale lines, not books on the shelf.

choices.text: The website holds 42.6% of the rows
choices.why: Right. Its node does 42.6% of the work and everybody waits for it.

prompt: A table is spread evenly by date, yet one node does most of the work. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: The hash function is broken
choices.why: The rows are even, so the hash is fine.

choices.text: Every query asks about the last week
choices.why: Right. Skewed queries: the nodes holding last week do all the work.

choices.text: Dates have too many distinct values
choices.why: Many values help balance; they do not cause skew.

choices.text: The dimensions are broadcast
choices.why: Broadcasting copies small tables to every node evenly.

prompt: The shop layout's fullest node has 643,004 rows; the average is 221,869. What is the skew ratio? Give one decimal.
Match each join strategy to what moves.
hint: Nothing, the small side, or both sides.

pairs.right: Nothing: matching rows already share a node
The small table, copied to every node
Both sides, re-spread by the join key

prompt: Why does a star schema suit an MPP system well?
hint: What is large and what is small?

choices.text: Big facts spread; small dimensions copy
choices.why: Right. 9,000 book rows copied instead of 666,023 sales moved.

choices.text: Stars have no joins
choices.why: They have one per dimension.

choices.text: Stars are always distributed by date
choices.why: Date is a common partition, a poor distribution key.

choices.text: MPP systems only accept stars
choices.why: They accept any schema; stars just suit them.

prompt: How many rows does broadcasting the 3,000-book table to the other three of four nodes move?
Sales and payments are both large and joined on `order_id` every night. How should they be distributed?

choices.text: Both broadcast to every node
choices.why: Broadcasting two large tables copies everything everywhere.

choices.text: Sales by shop and payments by method
choices.why: Few values, skewed nodes, and every join shuffles.

choices.text: Both by `order_id`, so the join is co-located
choices.why: Right. Spend the distribution key on the join between two large tables.

choices.text: By date, so March sits together
choices.why: That is a partitioning idea, and it leaves the join to shuffle.

prompt: What is the difference between distribution and partitioning?

choices.text: They are two names for one thing
choices.why: They do different jobs and combine.

choices.text: Machine against file
choices.why: Right. One spreads work, the other lets queries skip.

choices.text: Partitioning applies to dimensions only
choices.why: Fact tables are the usual thing to partition.

choices.text: Distribution only exists in the cloud
choices.why: MPP systems distributed data long before the cloud.

prompt: Asking for March 2025, how many of the 24 monthly files did DuckDB read?
Why not partition the sales by day instead of by month?
hint: Opening a file has a fixed cost.

choices.text: DuckDB cannot read 731 folders
choices.why: It can; it would just pay to open each small file.

choices.text: Nobody filters by day
choices.why: People do; the cost is in the files.

choices.text: Days are not a column of the sales
choices.why: `date_key` is a day.

choices.text: Tiny files cost more than they save
choices.why: Right. Too fine is as bad as too coarse.

prompt: What does separating storage from compute let a warehouse do that shared nothing makes hard?

choices.text: Store data by column
choices.why: Shared-nothing systems store by column too.

choices.text: Run joins without any network
choices.why: Compute still reads files over the network.

choices.text: Resize compute, data untouched
choices.why: Right. Elasticity, and isolation between teams.

choices.text: Avoid paying for storage
choices.why: Storage is still billed, by the gigabyte-month.

prompt: A customer table of 8 million rows will be spread across 16 nodes. Which distribution key is best?

choices.text: The customer id
choices.why: Right. Eight million distinct values hash evenly.

choices.text: The customer's state
choices.why: Twenty-seven values, and São Paulo alone would swamp one node.

choices.text: The loyalty tier
choices.why: Three values for sixteen nodes: thirteen would be idle.

choices.text: The date the customer joined
choices.why: Recent dates hold most customers, and queries about new joiners hit few nodes.
